claims.claim: Stress during adulthood leads to resetting of heritable silencing in the next generation.
claims.source: We found that, as was observed when stress was applied during the L1 stage, stress during adulthood leads to resetting of heritable silencing in the next generation (q < 0.0001, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: When stress was applied two generations after the parental exposure to dsRNA, no statistically significant stress-induced resetting was detected.
claims.source: In contrast, when stress was applied two generations after the parental exposure to dsRNA (P0: initiation of inheritance, F1: no stress, F2: stress), we did not detect statistically significant stress-induced resetting (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: The fate of the heritable response (its persistence across generations) is determined at the first generations.
claims.source: We previously showed that the fate of the heritable response (its persistence across generations) is determined at the first generations (Houri-Zeevi et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claims.claim: Re-challenging the F1 generation – but not the F2 generation – with RNAi extends the duration of ancestral RNAi responses.
claims.source: and that re-challenging the F1 generation – but not the F2 generation – with RNAi extends the duration of ancestral RNAi responses (Houri-Zeevi and Rechavi, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claims.claim: There exists a critical period at the F1 generation, during which the heritable response is still plastic and can be modified by external perturbations.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate the existence of a critical period at the F1 generation, during which the heritable response is still plastic and can be modified by external perturbations.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that stress at F1 but not F2 affects inheritance.

claims.claim: All three stressors (Heat, Osmotic, and Starvation stress) reset both endo-siRNAs- and piRNAs-mediated heritable silencing in worms that were directly exposed to stress.
claims.source: We found that all three stressors (Heat, Osmotic, and Starvation stress) reset both endo-siRNAs- and piRNAs-mediated heritable silencing in worms that were directly exposed to stress (Dunn's test, q-value <0.0005 and q-value <0.0007, respectively. See Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: Unstressed worms in the next generations re-established endo-siRNAs- and piRNAs-mediated silencing.
claims.source: However, in contrast to exo-siRNAs-mediated silencing that was reset in a transgenerational manner (Figure 1C), we found that unstressed worms in the next generations re-established endo-siRNAs- and piRNAs-mediated silencing.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing exo-siRNAs and endo-siRNAs/piRNAs responses.

claims.claim: Primary endo-siRNAs and piRNAs are encoded in the genome and do not depend on exogenous sources for their existence.
claims.source: Unlike exogenous primary small RNAs which cannot be re-synthesized in the progeny, primary endo-siRNAs and piRNAs are encoded in the genome and do not depend on exogenous sources for their existence (Ambros et al., 2003; Cecere et al., 2012; Duchaine et al., 2006; Gu et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2006; Lemmens and Tijsterman, 2011; Ruby et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: The re-establishment of endo-siRNAs and piRNAs-mediated silencing in the next generations after stress indicates that these small RNAs can be transcribed de novo at each generation.
claims.source: The re-establishment of endo-siRNAs and piRNAs-mediated silencing in the next generations after stress indicates that these small RNAs can be transcribed de novo at each generation, and thus can compensate for stress-induced erasure of parental small RNA molecules
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation of re-establishment of silencing.

claims.claim: There is a fundamental difference in the 'memory programs' of exogenous and endogenous transgenerational small RNA responses.
claims.source: suggesting a fundamental difference in the 'memory programs' of exogenous and endogenous transgenerational small RNA responses.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the different behaviors of exogenous and endogenous small RNA responses to stress.

claims.claim: Resetting only occurs in response to stress; progeny of stressed worms that were transferred to non-stressful conditions did not exhibit resetting of the heritable response.
claims.source: We found that resetting only occurs in response to stress (q-value <0.0001, Figure 3A); Progeny of stressed worms that were transferred to non-stressful conditions did not exhibit resetting of the heritable response.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Two consecutive generations of mild stress led to a weaker inheritance compared to worms that were not exposed to stress at all.
claims.source: Moreover, two consecutive generations of mild stress led to a weaker inheritance compared to worms that were not exposed to stress at all (q-value <0.0001, Figure 3A)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: RNAi responses initiated in stressed parents were strengthened when the progeny were transferred to non-stressful conditions.
claims.source: and RNAi responses initiated in stressed parents were strengthened when the progeny were transferred to non-stressful conditions (q-value <0.0053, Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Stress, and not any change in growth conditions, leads to the resetting of heritable small RNA responses, even regardless of the ancestral growth conditions.
claims.source: Overall, we conclude that stress, and not any change in growth conditions, leads to the resetting of heritable small RNA responses, even regardless of the ancestral growth conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that only stress, not environmental change, causes resetting.

claims.claim: Exposure to stress (starvation), even prior to the initiation of inheritance (for either one or three consecutive generations), leads to a similar resetting response as observed for stress that is applied in the next generation.
claims.source: Instead, we found that exposure to stress (starvation), even prior to the initiation of inheritance (for either one or three consecutive generations), leads to a similar resetting response as observed for stress that is applied in the next generation (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Stress inheritance can compete with other transgenerational responses, or affect the function of small RNA machinery in a transgenerational manner.
claims.source: These results indicate that stress inheritance can in fact compete with other transgenerational responses, or, alternatively, affect the function of small RNA machinery in a transgenerational manner (see Figure 3B and Discussion).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that pre-exposure to stress affects later heritable responses.

claims.claim: All three types of stress conditions led to a reduction in the levels of heritable endogenous small RNA in worms that were directly exposed to stress.
claims.source: Consistently with the observed phenotypic resetting of heritable responses following stress, in worms that were directly exposed to stress, all three types of stress conditions led to a reduction in the levels of heritable endogenous small RNA.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data.

claims.claim: Different stressors shaped the small RNA pools of the next generation in different ways.
claims.source: However, across multiple repeats (see Materials and methods), different stressors shaped the small RNA pools of the next generation in different ways (Figure 4B)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Starvation stress led to a reduction in endogenous small RNA levels both in the worms that were directly exposed to stress and in their progeny.
claims.source: starvation stress led to a reduction in endogenous small RNA levels both in the worms that were directly exposed to stress and in their progeny.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data.

claims.claim: Heat stress caused a reduction in endogenous small RNA levels in the stressed generation, but most types of endogenous small RNA showed elevated levels in the next generation after heat stress.
claims.source: In contrast, heat stress caused a reduction in endogenous small RNA levels in the stressed generation, but most types of endogenous small RNA showed elevated levels in the next generation after heat stress (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: No consistent heritable change in the global levels of endogenous small RNAs was detected following hyperosmotic stress.
claims.source: We did not detect a consistent heritable change in the global levels of endogenous small RNAs following hyperosmotic stress (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: 281 genes were identified as being targeted by stress-affected endogenous small RNAs.
claims.source: To better explore how stress-induced resetting affects each pathway, we examined stress-induced changes in small RNA regulation over specific genes and identified a list of 281 genes that were targeted by stress-affected endogenous small RNAs (regardless of the stress type. FDR < 0.1, Figure 4C and D, Supplementary file 1 and Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: The targets of stress-affected small RNAs show enrichment for stress-related functions.
claims.source: Interestingly, the targets of these stress-affected small RNAs show enrichment for stress-related functions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of the identified gene targets.

claims.claim: Stress-affected small RNA target genes were shown to be regulated by the TGF-beta pathway and the insulin pathway, and to be affected in response to rapamycin exposure and changes in temperature.
claims.source: As a group, these genes were shown to be regulated by the TGF-beta pathway and the insulin pathway, and to be affected in response to rapamycin exposure and changes in temperature (Calvert et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2015; Shaw et al., 2007; Viñuela et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: In most of the gene targets of stress-affected small RNAs (202/281, 72%) the targeting small RNAs were down-regulated, or 'reset', following stress.
claims.source: In agreement with the observed overall reduction in endogenous small RNA levels and the phenotypic resetting of the silencing responses, in most of the gene targets of stress-affected small RNAs (202/281, 72%) the targeting small RNAs were down-regulated, or 'reset', following stress.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data analysis.

claims.claim: Endogenous small RNAs that were reset following stress exhibited a strong enrichment for hrde-1-dependent small RNAs and Mutator-dependent small RNAs.
claims.source: These endogenous small RNAs exhibited a strong enrichment for hrde-1-dependent small RNAs and Mutator-dependent small RNAs (Phillips et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2011) (see Figure 4C and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4C and E.

claims.claim: The HRDE-1 (Heritable RNAi Deficient-1) Argonaute is an important regulator of transgenerational gene silencing by small RNAs and is explicitly required for transmission of silencing responses across generations.
claims.source: The HRDE-1 (Heritable RNAi Deficient-1) Argonaute is an important regulator of transgenerational gene silencing by small RNAs and, while largely dispensable for silencing within the same generation, is explicitly required for transmission of silencing responses across generations (Ashe et al., 2012; Buckley et al., 2012; Shirayama et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: The Mutator proteins are involved in multiple endogenous small RNA biogenesis pathways, affecting both somatic and germline small RNAs, and are required for efficient small RNA amplification and cleavage of target RNAs.
claims.source: The Mutator proteins (mut-16, mut-14;smut-1 Phillips et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2011) were shown to be involved in multiple endogenous small RNA biogenesis pathways, affecting both somatic and germline small RNAs, and are required for efficient small RNA amplification and cleavage of target RNAs (rde-8 and nyn-1;nyn-2 Tsai et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: Generating mut-14;smut-1;mut-16 triple mutants enables erasure of heritable small RNA-based memory of self and non-self-genes.
claims.source: Generating (via crossing) mut-14;smut-1;mut-16 triple mutants was previously shown to enable erasure of heritable small RNA-based memory of self and non-self-genes (de Albuquerque et al., 2015; Phillips et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: Targets of stress-reduced small RNAs are enriched for dsRNA-producing loci and piRNAs gene targets.
claims.source: Additionally, we found here that targets of stress-reduced small RNAs are enriched for dsRNA-producing loci (Saldi et al., 2014) and piRNAs gene targets (Bagijn et al., 2012) (see the full list of enrichments in Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis of small RNA sequencing data.

claims.claim: The targets of small RNAs that showed elevated levels following stress (79/281, 28%) were almost exclusively CSR-1-dependent endo-siRNAs.
claims.source: In contrast to the enrichment of HRDE-1 and Mutator-dependent small RNAs among small RNAs which are reset following stress, the targets of small RNAs that showed elevated levels of small RNAs following stress (79/281, 28%) were almost exclusively CSR-1-dependent endo-siRNAs (hypergeometric test, p-value=2.9 e−48, 96% were found to be physically bound to CSR-1, Claycomb et al., 2009; Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Endo-siRNAs which are bound by the CSR-1 Argonaute promote gene expression rather than gene silencing in the worms.
claims.source: Unlike other endo-siRNAs pathways, endo-siRNAs which are bound by the CSR-1 Argonaute were demonstrated to promote gene expression rather than gene silencing in the worms (Wedeles et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claims.claim: Only 10 genes were targeted by small RNAs that showed widespread changes in the progeny of stressed worms, when accounting for all stress types together.
claims.source: Finally, we did not detect widespread changes in stress-affected small RNAs in the progeny of stressed worms, when accounting for all stress types together (only 10 genes were targeted by such small RNAs, Supplementary file 2)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data analysis.

claims.claim: Multiple epigenetic, small RNA, and p-granules factors consistently show significantly reduced gene expression levels following stress, regardless of the stress types.
claims.source: We found that multiple epigenetic, small RNA, and p-granules factors consistently show significantly reduced gene expression levels following stress, regardless of the stress types (73 epigenetic-related genes significantly downregulated in all stress conditions with FDR < 0.1, Supplementary file 4, hypergeometric test; fold-enrichment = 2.4, adjusted p-value<0.00001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published mRNA-sequencing data.

claims.claim: The Argonaute genes hrde-1, rde-1, ergo-1, nrde-3, wago-1, and alg-2 are all significantly downregulated across all stress types.
claims.source: Specifically, we found that the Argonaute genes hrde-1, rde-1, ergo-1, nrde-3, wago-1, and alg-2 are all significantly downregulated across all stress types.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published mRNA-sequencing data.

claims.claim: The Argonautes hrde-1, rde-1, ergo-1, nrde-3, wago-1, and alg-2 regulate and are necessary for RNAi responses both within and across generations.
claims.source: These Argonautes were previously shown to regulate and be necessary for RNAi responses both within and across generations (Buckley et al., 2012; Billi et al., 2014; Grishok et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: The Mutator genes mut-2 and mut-16, and the factors rde-4, rrf-3, hrde-4, and rde-8 all show significantly reduced gene expression levels in response to stress.
claims.source: Additionally, we found that the Mutator genes mut-2 and mut-16, whose small RNAs were depleted following stress, and the factors rde-4, rrf-3, hrde-4, and rde-8 all show significantly reduced gene expression levels in response to stress (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published mRNA-sequencing data.

claims.claim: The epigenetic factors rde-4, rrf-3, hrde-4, and rde-8 are required for the synthesis, amplification, and inheritance of small RNAs across generations.
claims.source: These epigenetic factors were previously found to be required for the synthesis, amplification, and inheritance of small RNAs across generations (Duchaine et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2006; Parker, 2006; Spracklin et al., 2017; Tabara et al., 2002; Tsai et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: Stress induces a widespread suppression of various components of the small RNA machinery.
claims.source: Overall, we find that stress induces a widespread suppression of various components of the small RNA machinery, in accordance with the observed global resetting of small RNA responses and multiple types of endogenous small RNAs (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the mRNA-seq data analysis showing downregulation of small RNA machinery components.

claims.claim: Eight mutants defective in stress responses showed a general enhanced or defective RNAi inheritance, irrespectively of whether the mutant worms experienced stress or not.
claims.source: Interestingly, out of the 11 mutants defective in stress responses that we examined, eight mutants showed a general enhanced (pmk-1/p38 MAPK, sek-1/p38 MAP2K, skn-1/Nrf2, daf-2/InsR) or defective (mek-1;sek-1, kgb-1, daf-2/InsR;daf-16/FOXO, hsf-1/HSF1) RNAi inheritance (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2). This was true irrespectively of whether the mutant worms experienced stress or not
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claims.claim: Stress regulation and small RNA inheritance are interconnected even in the absence of stress.
claims.source: and suggests that stress regulation and small RNA inheritance are interconnected even in the absence of stress.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that stress pathway mutants show altered RNAi inheritance even without stress.

claims.claim: MAP Kinase (MAPK) genes (sek-1/mek-1, sek-1, pmk-1, kgb-1), and the skn-1 gene are required for resetting of RNAi inheritance in response to stress.
claims.source: We found that MAP Kinase (MAPK) genes (sek-1/mek-1, sek-1, pmk-1, kgb-1), and the skn-1 gene are required for resetting of RNAi inheritance in response to stress (Figure 5B and C, and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C, and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claims.claim: skn-1/Nrf2 encodes a transcription factor which is regulated by p38 MAPK-dependent phosphorylation.
claims.source: skn-1/Nrf2 encodes a transcription factor which is regulated by p38 MAPK-dependent phosphorylation (Inoue et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claims.claim: All the examined mutant worms expressed the GFP transgene in similar levels to wild-type worms in the absence of anti-gfp RNAi response.
claims.source: Importantly, all the examined mutant worms expressed the GFP transgene in similar levels to wild-type worms in the absence of anti-gfp RNAi response (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: HSF-1 activity corresponds to the 'inheritance state' of worms when initiating a heritable RNAi response.
claims.source: We recently showed that HSF-1 activity corresponds to the 'inheritance state' of worms when initiating a heritable RNAi response (Houri-Zeevi et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claims.claim: The finding that hsf-1 mutants are capable of resetting RNAi inheritance in response to stress suggests that HSF-1's role is likely in the initiation, and not the maintenance, of heritable RNAi responses.
claims.source: Our finding that hsf-1 mutants are capable of resetting RNAi inheritance in response to stress suggests that HSF-1's role is likely in the initiation, and not the maintenance, of heritable RNAi responses.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that hsf-1 mutants can still reset RNAi inheritance.

claims.claim: The MAPK pathway is necessary for the integration of responses to multiple types of stress, such as DNA damage, osmotic stress, heat shock, and pathogen infection.
claims.source: The MAPK pathway is necessary for the integration of responses to multiple types of stress, such as DNA damage (Bianco and Schumacher, 2018; Ermolaeva et al., 2013), osmotic stress (Gerke et al., 2014), heat shock (Mertenskötter et al., 2013), and pathogen infection (Troemel et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: The ability to reset heritable responses following stress, and the ability to transmit RNAi, appear to be two distinct functions.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that the ability to reset heritable responses following stress, and the ability to transmit RNAi, appear to be two distinct functions
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that different mutants show different patterns of RNAi inheritance and resetting.

claims.claim: Some of the mutants that did not reset heritable silencing following stress showed enhanced RNAi inheritance (sek-1, pmk-1, skn-1, acting in the same signaling cascade), while others were defective in RNAi inheritance (mek-1/sek-1 and kgb-1).
claims.source: some of the mutants that did not reset heritable silencing following stress showed enhanced RNAi inheritance (sek-1, pmk-1, skn-1, acting in the same signaling cascade), while others were defective in RNAi inheritance (mek-1/sek-1 and kgb-1) (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Resetting of heritable silencing following stress is a regulated process that is mediated by the MAPK pathway and by the skn-1 transcription factor.
claims.source: Overall, we conclude that resetting of heritable silencing following stress is a regulated process that is mediated by the MAPK pathway and by the skn-1 transcription factor.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that MAPK pathway and skn-1 mutants cannot reset RNAi inheritance.

claims.claim: Neuronal expression of sek-1 is sufficient to re-establish a strong resetting of silencing in response to stress.
claims.source: We found that neuronal expression of sek-1 is sufficient to re-establish a strong resetting of silencing in response to stress (Figure 5D, Cliff's Delta = 0.4597, 0.593, 0.2672 for heat stress, hyperosmotic stress, and starvation stress, respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Intestinal rescue of sek-1 did not regenerate a strong resetting response following heat stress and starvation stress, but did regenerate a strong resetting response following osmotic stress.
claims.source: Intestinal rescue of sek-1, on the other hand, did not regenerate a strong resetting response following heat stress and starvation stress (Cliff's Delta = 0.0905, 0.0909), but did regenerate a strong resetting response following osmotic stress (Cliff's Delta = 0.4108).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with effect size measurements.

claims.claim: Osmotic stress is the only stress condition that did not show a consistent effect on the total small RNA pools in unstressed progeny.
claims.source: Notably, osmotic stress is the only stress condition that did not show a consistent effect on the total small RNA pools in unstressed progeny (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Unlike starvation and heat stress, osmotic stress was shown to elicit an intergenerational, and not a transgenerational, epigenetic response.
claims.source: Moreover, unlike starvation and heat stress, osmotic stress was shown to elicit an intergenerational, and not a transgenerational, epigenetic response (Burton et al., 2017; Rechavi et al., 2014; Schott et al., 2015), that is mediated through the intestine.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: While many stress-related factors in the worm affect the basic function of the RNAi inheritance machinery, the p38 MAPK pathway – and the SKN-1/Nrf2 transcription factor which is regulated by it – are specifically required for resetting of small RNAs in response to stress.
claims.source: Overall, we conclude that while many stress-related factors in the worm affect the basic function of the RNAi inheritance machinery (Figure 5A), the p38 MAPK pathway – and the SKN-1/Nrf2 transcription factor which is regulated by it – are specifically required for resetting of small RNAs in response to stress.

results.result: Stress applied at the F1 generation, but not F2, resets exogenous dsRNA-derived heritable silencing in a transgenerational manner. This defines a critical period at F1 during which heritable responses remain plastic and modifiable by external perturbations.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C28 collectively demonstrate that stress at F1 (both L1 and adult stages) resets heritable silencing across multiple generations (F1-F5), while stress at F2 has no effect. The experimental data (Figures 1, 1-supplement 3-5) with statistical support (q<0.0001) and prior work (C26-C27) converge to establish a critical F1 window for modulating inheritance.

results.result: Stress resets endogenous siRNA- and piRNA-mediated silencing within the same generation, but these responses re-establish in unstressed progeny due to genomic encoding of primary small RNAs, revealing fundamental differences between exogenous and endogenous small RNA memory programs.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 show that all three stressors reset endo-siRNA and piRNA silencing in stressed worms (q<0.0007, Figure 2), but unlike exogenous responses, these re-establish in F2 because primary endo-siRNAs/piRNAs are genome-encoded (C31). The mechanistic explanation (C32) and conclusion (C33) are well-supported by the contrasting behaviors observed.

results.result: Stress itself, not environmental change per se, drives resetting of heritable small RNA responses. Continuous mild stress weakens inheritance while transfer from stress to non-stress strengthens it.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 demonstrate through controlled experiments (Figure 3A) that only stress exposure—not shifts between conditions—causes resetting (q<0.0001). The complementary findings that continuous stress weakens (C35) and stress-to-control transfer strengthens (C36) inheritance provide strong evidence for stress-specific rather than change-dependent effects.

results.result: Pre-exposure to stress (before RNAi initiation) reduces subsequent heritable responses, suggesting stress inheritance can compete with other transgenerational responses or affect small RNA machinery transgenerationally.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 show that stress applied 1-3 generations before RNAi initiation produces similar resetting as post-initiation stress (Figure 3B). While the mechanistic interpretation (C39) is somewhat speculative (competition vs. machinery effects), the experimental observation is clear and statistically supported.

results.result: Stress induces genome-wide reduction in endogenous small RNA levels in directly exposed worms, but different stressors produce distinct heritable effects: starvation causes sustained reduction, heat stress causes rebound elevation in F2, and osmotic stress shows no consistent heritable changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 are supported by small RNA-seq data (Figure 4B) across multiple biological replicates. The stress-specific patterns in progeny (C41-C44) are clearly documented, though the lack of consistent osmotic effects (C44) may reflect biological variability or the intergenerational (vs transgenerational) nature of osmotic responses.

results.result: 281 genes targeted by stress-affected small RNAs show enrichment for stress-related functions. 72% of these show downregulated small RNAs enriched for HRDE-1 and Mutator-dependent pathways, which are critical for transgenerational inheritance and small RNA amplification.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C53 present comprehensive small RNA-seq analysis (FDR<0.1, Figure 4C-E) identifying specific gene targets and pathway enrichments. The functional enrichment (C46-C47), quantitative breakdown (C48), and pathway-specific enrichments (C49, C53) are well-documented. The biological context from prior work (C50-C52) strengthens interpretation.

results.result: Small RNAs showing elevated levels after stress (28% of targets) are almost exclusively CSR-1-dependent endo-siRNAs that promote rather than silence gene expression. Few genes show consistent heritable changes across all stress types.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by small RNA-seq analysis showing 96% of upregulated targets are CSR-1-bound (p=2.9e-48, Figure 4E) and that CSR-1 promotes expression (C55). The limited heritable changes (only 10 genes, C56) are clearly stated with appropriate caveats about stress-type specificity.

results.result: Stress induces widespread transcriptional suppression of small RNA machinery components across all stress types, including multiple Argonaute genes (hrde-1, rde-1, ergo-1, nrde-3, wago-1, alg-2), Mutator genes, and other epigenetic factors required for small RNA synthesis, amplification, and inheritance.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C62 present mRNA-seq analysis showing 73 epigenetic genes downregulated (FDR<0.1, fold-enrichment=2.4, p<0.00001). Specific genes (C58, C60) are identified with functional context from prior work (C59, C61). The conclusion (C62) appropriately synthesizes these findings as a coordinated suppression mechanism.

results.result: The p38 MAPK pathway (sek-1, pmk-1, kgb-1) and SKN-1/Nrf2 transcription factor are specifically required for stress-induced resetting of RNAi inheritance. Stress pathway mutants show altered RNAi inheritance even without stress, indicating interconnection between stress regulation and small RNA inheritance.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C73 present systematic mutant analysis (Figures 5A-C, supplements 1-2) showing 8/11 stress mutants have altered inheritance baselines (C63-C64) and that MAPK/SKN-1 mutants specifically cannot reset (C65, C73). Controls confirm equal GFP expression (C67). The distinction between resetting ability and inheritance capacity (C71-C72) is well-documented, though HSF-1's role interpretation (C69) is somewhat inferential.

results.result: Neuronal expression of sek-1 is sufficient to restore stress-induced resetting for most stresses (effect sizes 0.27-0.59), while intestinal rescue only restores osmotic stress resetting (effect size 0.41). This suggests tissue-specific regulation, with osmotic stress uniquely acting through intestine consistent with its intergenerational (not transgenerational) nature.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 present tissue-specific rescue experiments (Figure 5D) with appropriate effect size reporting (Cliff's Delta) given large sample size (N=3193). The neuronal sufficiency (C74) is well-supported, though intestinal results (C75) are complicated by generally low silencing. The osmotic stress distinction (C76-C77) provides biological context for differential tissue requirements.

results.result: SKN-1 regulates expression of multiple epigenetic and small RNA factors. Genes showing SKN-1-dependent stress repression are enriched for epigenetic factors (35/599 genes, q<0.001), including nrde-3, rrf-3, rde-8, and nyn-2. SKN-1 binding sites are found in promoters of rrf-3 and met-2.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 integrate mRNA-seq analysis of skn-1 knockdown with motif analysis. The enrichment statistics (C81) and specific gene identification (C82-C83) are well-documented. However, C79 and C84 are somewhat speculative about direct regulation—the evidence shows correlation and binding site presence but not direct functional validation of SKN-1-mediated regulation.

results.result: MET-2 (H3K9 methyltransferase) is essential for stress-induced resetting of heritable RNAi. Stress-affected small RNA targets are enriched for genes misregulated in met-2 mutants (FDR=2.1e-05) and show elevated H3K9me2. met-2 expression is downregulated by all stress types, and met-2 mutants are completely resistant to stress-induced resetting.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C106 integrate prior knowledge (C99-C100), bioinformatic analysis (C101-C102), expression data (C103), and experimental validation (C104-C105, Figure 6B, supplement 1B). The convergent evidence from multiple approaches strongly supports MET-2's role in executing resetting, though the precise mechanism remains to be elucidated.

results.result: Stress resets transgenerationally transmitted small RNAs through p38 MAPK pathway, SKN-1 transcription factor, and MET-2 H3K9 methyltransferase, causing genome-wide reduction in multiple distinct small RNA species including those regulating stress-related genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C89 are summary statements synthesizing the major findings. These are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout (small RNA-seq, mutant analysis, mRNA-seq). The claims appropriately integrate the mechanistic (C86-C87) and molecular (C88-C89) findings.

results.result: Stress-induced resetting of heritable small RNAs could be adaptive in changing environments by increasing phenotypic plasticity or revealing hidden genetic variability through relief of small RNA-mediated buffering.
results.evaluation: Claims C90, C91, and C94 are explicitly speculative statements about potential adaptive significance. While the speculation is reasonable given the data, no direct evidence for adaptive value, increased variability, or fitness consequences is provided. These remain hypotheses requiring future experimental validation.

results.result: Non-DNA-based inheritance may be involved in human disorders, but conservation of worm mechanisms in mammals is unclear. If conserved, understanding resetting pathways could aid disease prevention or treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 discuss translational implications but acknowledge major uncertainties. C107 is supported by citations but remains correlative. C108 explicitly states mechanisms are unclear in mammals. C109 is conditional speculation. These appropriately frame potential significance while acknowledging the large gap between C. elegans findings and human applications.

results.result: Human imprinting disorders and widespread diseases may be influenced by non-genetic inheritance of parental information.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 provide background context supported by multiple citations. These establish the broader significance of studying non-genetic inheritance mechanisms, though they represent prior work rather than findings of this study.

results.result: C. elegans has well-characterized mechanisms for transgenerational small RNA inheritance involving specific Argonaute proteins, RdRPs, germ granules, and chromatin regulators that respond to environmental challenges and are actively regulated across generations.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C13 provide comprehensive background on small RNA inheritance mechanisms in C. elegans, all supported by multiple citations to prior work. These establish the foundation for understanding the current study's findings but represent established knowledge rather than new results.

results.result: Heritable RNAi responses in C. elegans typically last 3-5 generations but vary among individuals and mutants. MET-2 is required for termination, and inheritance can be extended by various manipulations. Unregulated accumulation leads to sterility.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C22 provide essential background on RNAi inheritance dynamics and regulation, supported by citations to prior work including authors' own studies. These establish the experimental system and biological context but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: Small RNAs in C. elegans distinguish self from non-self, regulate germline gene expression, and can buffer developmental variation. Neuronal small RNAs and olfactory memory can be heritable, with stress responses coordinated by the nervous system.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93, C95-C98 provide relevant background from prior work (all citation-supported) that contextualizes the discussion of mechanisms and potential functions. These support the interpretation of findings but are not results of this study.
